comment:
As of today, how long would it take us to build all of that? Just to construct a single one, including excavating a 30-meter-deep underground section, creating the chambers, carving everything perfectly, with inscriptions and artwork? And then aligning it with Orion's Belt...
Yeah, people say it was the Egyptians. It's not about conspiracy theories, but I don't believe fairy tales. It would have taken millions and millions of people just to build one. Then there's the fact that the materials were transported from miles and miles away. The massive stone blocks are fitted together so precisely that you can't even slip a sheet of paper between them.
Even today, it would be an enormous challenge for humanity to transport and build something like that. Personally, I'd sooner believe the "alien" explanation than the story that it was all done by the ancient Egyptians.

comment:
I asked AI: What is the volume of the Suez canal?
That’s a good question — the exact “volume” of water in the Suez Canal depends on which parts you include. But we can make a rough estimate using published dimensions.

✅ Known dimensions
Length: ~ 193.3 km (as of recent configuration). Encyclopedia Britannica+2Suez Canal Authority+2

Maximum water depth: ~ 24 m. Suez Canal Authority+1

Typical surface-width / canal width: water-surface width can be ~ 313 m, while a narrower “navigational channel” is often 200–210 m wide. World Economic Forum+2Alexandria Chamber of Shipping+2

🔢 Rough volume estimate (upper bound)
If we approximate the canal cross-section as a rectangle of 24 m depth × 313 m width — multiplied by 193.3 km length — we get:

Volume≈193,300m×313m×24m≈1.45×10^9 m3
That’s about 1.4 billion cubic meters of water (assuming uniform maximum width & depth).
This means that approximately 14,500,000 m³ of stone blocks were removed to dig the canal. Those materials would have had to be placed somewhere: either piled up along the canal as a wall with the same width and height as the canal’s depth, or stacked into large pyramid-shaped structures. We chose the latter.
